headline: When markets learn to simulate themselves.
standfirst: A research dispatch on probabilistic order books, synthetic markets and the difficult distance between a convincing model and a trustworthy decision.
opening: The most compelling question in this edition is not whether machines can model financial markets. It is whether those models preserve the details that matter once a forecast becomes an order, an allocation or a risk decision.
takeaway: The next frontier is not simulation alone. It is proving that simulated behaviour survives calibration, market impact, changing regimes and the tails.

themes.desc: Generative order books, learned market states and strategic liquidity models.
Synthetic scenarios and risk-sensitive allocation expose fragile assumptions.
Filtering and posterior uncertainty connect information to trading decisions.

priorities.headline: Can a synthetic order book move like a real market?
priorities.summary: The LOB-Impact benchmark asks whether generative market models produce credible responses to injected trades — a stricter test than good-looking order-flow predictions.
priorities.limitation: Author-reported tests span five neural generators and five NASDAQ stocks; the measured impact curves are not independent evidence of real execution quality.

priorities.headline: A forecast should know when it might be wrong.
priorities.summary: Neural filtering for statistical arbitrage points towards position sizing informed by the full uncertainty distribution rather than a single estimated spread.
priorities.limitation: Korean-equity results and controlled simulations do not establish general calibration or profitability in other instruments and regimes.

priorities.headline: The danger of believable synthetic scenarios.
priorities.summary: TimeGAN can produce plausible portfolio scenarios while understating volatility and tail dependence, potentially undermining tail-sensitive optimisation.
priorities.limitation: The negative result is tied to this generator, the 12-ETF setting and the evaluated Rachev-ratio strategies; it does not generalise to all synthetic-data methods.

synthesis_heading: Fidelity is only useful when it survives a decision.
synthesis: Across probabilistic prediction, generative microstructure and portfolio simulation, the common test is whether a model retains the features a decision depends on. Calibration, impact and tail behaviour form a more demanding standard than predictive fit alone.

experiment.headline: A synthetic-market fidelity audit
experiment.basis: Editorial proposal inspired by LOB-Impact, LOBGrad and TimeGAN; none of these papers verifies the proposed combined evaluation.
experiment.hypothesis: A model with strong predictive fit can nevertheless fail an execution-relevant calibration, market-impact or tail-risk test.
experiment.criterion: Compare held-out calibration, impact-response and tail statistics against explicit real-data baselines; reject the hypothesis only if the synthetic system meets pre-specified tolerances across all three.
